title: Physical Tests
summary:
Physical assessment before starting an exercise program lets a trainer personalize intensity, duration and type of activity. Tests must be safe, validated and adapted to the physiological, biomechanical and hormonal changes of pregnancy. The chapter notes that many common tests are too intense for pregnant women, and that the literature is inconclusive about which protocols to use.

The chapter focuses on low-cost field tests, since laboratory tests are the gold standard but costly. It reviews tests for cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, flexibility, speed and balance, and says pelvic floor assessment belongs to physiotherapists. It concludes that a pregnancy-specific, validated test battery is needed, because most current tests are adaptations from other populations.
points: A systematic review found fitness during pregnancy was measured with 75 cardiorespiratory protocols, 16 muscular, 13 flexibility and 40 balance protocols, often lacking validity and reliability.
Tests should be repeated every 2-3 months and the data recorded to assess progress, with a warm-up and stable conditions (time, food, rest).
The 6-Minute Walk Test uses a 30-meter corridor at a comfortable pace, with heart rate monitored and RPE of 12-14 recommended.
The Modified Step Test uses a 15-20 cm step for 3 min at a controlled pace, measuring heart rate afterward.
The Modified Balke treadmill protocol (validated by Mottola et al.) suits trained women and athletes without contraindications, but needs a treadmill.
The Chair Stand Test lasts 30 s without using the arms; handgrip dynamometry gives a general indicator of strength, but a maximal isometric test should not be used.
In the Modified Sit-and-Reach Test a range greater than 20 cm is adequate; the Back Scratch Test and goniometry assess shoulder and joint mobility.
Speed testing (10 m timed walk) is not ideal because speed should not be a focus in pregnancy and is linked to sudden movements and fall risk.
The single-leg stance test is a simple, inexpensive field balance test; no articles on agility and coordination assessment were found.
takeaways: Use submaximal tests and never add risk during testing.
Sedentary beginners should use the 6MWT or Modified Step Test.
Trained women without contraindications may use the Modified Balke treadmill protocol if equipment is available.
Include lower-limb strength tests such as the chair stand test.
Do balance tests next to a wall or support bar under close supervision.
Repeat tests every 2-3 months and keep a record.
cautions: Discontinue testing if dizziness, pelvic pain, excessive shortness of breath or contractions occur.
Avoid prolonged supine positions after the second trimester and avoid bouncing or hyperextension in flexibility tests.
Pelvic floor assessment (e.g., PERFECT, biofeedback) must be done only by physiotherapists or qualified professionals.
